summary:
South Gyeongsang has no province-specific transgender ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding in these sources, so a visitor is assessed against the national framework of the Republic of Korea, which applies across the province.

South Korea does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The armed forces are the exception: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available and the surgery requirement has fallen. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved male-to-female registered-sex change for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change by surgery, that judicial guidelines requiring surgery are now reference rather than criteria, and that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. The Supreme Court has also allowed a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

Trans visitors have a judicially enforced right to public restrooms. In a case finalised on 22 July 2024 the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and confirmed a 300,000 won damages award against a claim of 3 million won, ruling that police advice telling a plaintiff transitioning from male to female to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights, and holding that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. That plaintiff had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020.

No comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on those grounds. In healthcare, the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner. The Constitutional Court's landmark 2024 ruling extending healthcare rights to same-sex partners grants recognition in that specific area only.

Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are broadly positive, but the surrounding context requires care: organised conservative opposition is active, no national anti-discrimination law exists, and Human Rights Watch records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in its 2025 world report, which also notes a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society. No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources.
tangentialFactors:
Restroom avoidance is routine rather than exceptional. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found 41% using a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoiding food and drink outlets, and 36% going without restroom use altogether, which indicates the practical exposure a visitor faces even where the law is on their side.

Institutional refusal has already produced damages elsewhere. In 2021 the Daegu District Court, Pohang branch, awarded 7 million won against a beauty academy that prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom.

The protections a trans visitor in South Gyeongsang relies on were established by courts in other provinces, Yeongdong on surgery-free sex change and Pohang on facilities access, alongside the Seoul ruling on police advice. The guarantees are national in reach rather than local in origin, and no province-level instrument in this province is on record either reinforcing or diluting them.

The military exception is a standing source of legal jeopardy for service members rather than for civilian visitors, but it shapes the surrounding climate: a provision the Constitutional Court chose to uphold in 2023 signals that conservative legal positions retain institutional support despite the pro-recognition rulings of 2024.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change is recorded in the family relations register, and since the 8 May 2024 Yeongdong ruling the surgical prerequisite has been treated as unlawful rather than as a criterion; the Supreme Court has separately permitted the register change for a transgender parent with minor children.

Transgender people are barred from military service, an exclusion that falls on residents of South Gyeongsang reaching service age and that sits alongside the criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct under Military Criminal Act article 92-6 for those who serve.

With no anti-discrimination statute covering gender identity, residents have no statutory claim in employment, education, healthcare or accommodation; recourse runs through the National Human Rights Commission of Korea, whose November 2023 intervention followed the Ministry of Health and Welfare's refusal to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients.

Police advice cannot lawfully restrict a person's access to public restrooms once gender recognition has been granted, on the authority of the finalised 2024 ruling awarding 300,000 won against the state.
outOfScopeNotes:
No South Gyeongsang-specific incident, ordinance or enforcement action involving a transgender person appears in these sources. Whether Gyeongsangnam-do or its police, education and health authorities have issued any trans-specific guidance, or whether any incident has occurred in the province, is unresolved in this record.

The sources do not establish how the surgery-free standard for registered-sex change is being applied by the district courts sitting in South Gyeongsang, or whether any of them has departed from the Yeongdong reasoning.

Whether any later appeal or Supreme Court decision after the May and July 2024 rulings altered the surgery requirement or the restroom holding is not sourced here.
